accuracy.evidence: Every lab quote was checked word for word against the Mia passage: 'Her hands shook', 'She bit her lip' and 'looked at the floor' are verbatim spans that prove nervousness, and 'Mia grinned' proves pride. The misquote 'Her hand was shaking as she held the poem' differs in exactly three places (hand, was shaking, the). The honeybee challenge answer is the only option that copies the article exactly and proves the distance claim.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips named in the adult text: quoting a whole paragraph (step 1 prediction), paraphrasing inside quotation marks and changing small words (step 2 misquote hunt, m4, p3), marks round the writer's own words such as 'nervous' (step 3 gap feedback, p4, m5), accurate words that prove nothing (challenge tag off, m3) and a bare quote with no explanation (step 5 tiles, m6, challenge tag bare).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built for this topic alone: learners drag across the words of a story to select a span, spot each changed word in Sam's copy, tap the gaps where quotation marks belong in their own sentence, and assemble signal phrase, quotation and explanation tiles. No other lesson has a text-selection or quotation-mark placement mechanic.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the learner do the skill: choose the fewest words that prove a claim, compare a copy to the source, place opening and closing marks round only copied words, and build a full answer sentence. Feedback after each attempt names the exact problem (too long, word changed, own words inside marks, no explanation), so the learner fixes it rather than guessing.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions come before the action: how much to quote, whether a same-meaning copy is fine, where the marks go, whether a quote can prove an unstated feeling, and what comes after a quotation. Each reveal reflects on the learner's own choice by name, so a wrong guess is turned into the reason the rule exists.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The honeybee challenge rotates options and tags each wrong answer: mis (changed word, 'further' for 'farther'), off (true words that do not prove the claim), bare (no explanation), fake (words not in the text). Every miss explains which rule broke and points to the earlier step that practises it.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs are short sentences with everyday words and checked against the 6.5 grade limit for the 10 to 11 band; adult notes stay under 9.5. Story texts are simple and concrete (curtain, poem, crowd) so the reading load sits on the quoting skill, not on hard vocabulary.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a rule, an example or a mistake: what to quote, copying exactly, where marks go, signal phrase and explanation. There are no motivational filler lines, and every item explanation states why the answer is right in terms of the source words.

mobile.evidence: Checked at iPhone 13 size: the passage wraps inside the canvas, word selection works by drag or by the Start and End buttons, mark placement works by tapping gaps or by buttons, and tiles work by drag or tap then tap a box. Buttons are full-size touch targets with no horizontal scroll.

accessibility.evidence: axe found no violations on any step in dark and light themes at desktop and phone sizes. Every gesture has a button alternative, the canvas has an aria-label that includes the passage and the current state, and results are announced through the live status line.

sources: UK National Curriculum English programmes of study, KS2 years 5 to 6: retrieve, record and present information; use inverted commas and other punctuation
Common Core ELA RL.5.1 and RI.5.1: quote accurately from a text when explaining what it says and when drawing inferences
Cambridge Primary English curriculum framework, stage 6 reading: use evidence from the text to support views
Read Write Think / NCTE guidance on the PEE (point, evidence, explain) and ICE (introduce, cite, explain) quotation structures
